data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological evolution has no goal of truth, whereas Popperian science explicitly aims at verisimilitude.","Natural selection operates blindly over eons, while scientific preference is a conscious, rapid, critical act.","Survival in nature implies reproductive fitness, while survival of a theory implies only that it hasn't been falsified yet."],"overturn_conditions":["If a less-tested theory consistently outperforms a highly corroborated one in practice, the link between corroboration and practical preference breaks.","If verisimilitude is proven logically incoherent, the normative force of choosing the 'most tested' theory vanishes."],"shared_structure":["Selection based on survival of stress tests rather than prediction of future performance.","Distinction between the logic of the filter and the utility of the filtered item.","Acceptance of a 'best available' option without claiming it is 'good' or 'true' in an absolute sense."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_004"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we trust a bridge that survived stress tests not because it's 'probable' to hold but because it's the only one not known to break, we prefer corroborated theories.","The 'rationality' of the choice lies in the rigor of the testing process, not in the outcome's guarantee."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible without smuggling in induction if 'preference' is redefined as a critical selection mechanism for maximizing testability (verisimilitude) rather than an inductive inference of future truth; however, this defense survives only by accepting the cost that scientific action becomes a non-rational 'leap of faith' regarding practical success, grounded solely in the logical asymmetry of falsification.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent requires a guarantee of practical success for action, Popper's framework fails, forcing a retreat to irrationalism or hidden induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be formally defined without probabilistic assumptions (as per Miller/Tich\u00fd), the logical basis for preferring one false theory over another collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on' a theory inherently implies believing it is more likely to succeed than alternatives, the distinction between logical corroboration and psychological expectation dissolves.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Reframe the scientist's choice not as predicting 'Theory T will work' (inductive probability) but as selecting 'Theory T is the most severely tested and thus currently closest to truth available' (critical rationalism). The preference is a procedural rule to expose error faster, not a guarantee of utility. The survival of the theory indicates it has withstood attempts to kill it, making it the best target for further criticism, not the most probable predictor.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
